query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying severe plastic deformation (SPD) processing to refine the grain structure of NbMoTaW will enhance room-temperature ductility and irradiation damage tolerance via increased grain boundary area acting as defect sinks, while largely preserving high-temperature properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Coarse-grained, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW characterized by high strength at elevated temperatures but very low room-temperature ductility (~2% plastic strain).
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to high-pressure torsion (HPT) at room temperature to achieve an ultrafine-grained structure, followed by a brief low-temperature annealing treatment to partially relieve internal stresses while retaining the fine grain size. Include a minor addition of a grain-growth inhibitor (e.g., trace refractory oxide) during melting to stabilize grain boundaries at high temperature.
generation.conditions: Samples are processed via HPT under controlled strain rates and rotations, then annealed in an inert atmosphere at low temperature. Subsequent evaluations include room-temperature tensile/compressive tests, high-temperature creep testing (up to 1600 °C), and He-ion irradiation experiments under reactor-relevant conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultrafine-grained microstructure with a high volume fraction of grain boundaries that act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
generation.mechanism: The ultrafine grain size increases the density of grain boundaries, which facilitate dislocation motion (enhancing ductility) and serve as efficient sinks for irradiation-induced point defects, reducing the formation of defect clusters. With the inclusion of a grain-growth inhibitor, the refined structure is expected to resist coarsening during high-temperature service, thereby maintaining high-temperature strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The SPD-processed, ultrafine-grained NbMoTaW alloy should exhibit a significant increase in room-temperature ductility and reduced irradiation defect density, with high-temperature yield and creep properties maintained at levels comparable to the coarse-grained baseline, provided grain coarsening is effectively inhibited.
generation.baseline: Standard, coarse-grained NbMoTaW presents low ductility (~2% plastic strain) and irradiation tolerance that is mainly supported by computational predictions.
generation.boundary: The enhanced properties are expected from room temperature up to moderate-high temperatures; however, at extreme temperatures approaching 1600 °C, the success depends on the effectiveness of the grain-growth inhibitor to prevent grain coarsening.
generation.uncertainty: While the role of increased grain boundary area as defect sinks is well supported, the long-term thermal stability of the ultrafine-grained microstructure in NbMoTaW under extremely high temperatures and irradiation must be rigorously validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Process NbMoTaW samples via HPT with and without the minor grain-growth inhibitor. Characterize the resulting grain size distribution using EBSD/TEM immediately after processing and after prolonged high-temperature exposure. Perform room-temperature mechanical tests and He-ion irradiation experiments to compare ductility and defect sink efficacy.
measurements: Grain size distribution and stability (EBSD/TEM) pre- and post-high-temperature exposure
High-temperature yield strength and creep performance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SPD-processed alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in ductility or if the ultrafine-grained structure coarsens markedly during high-temperature exposure (leading to diminished high-temperature strength or no reduction in irradiation defect density), the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: We introduce a novel transformation-induced plasticity mechanism, i.e., a martensitic transformation from fcc phase to bcc phase, in medium-entropy alloys (MEAs). A VCrFeCoNi MEA system is designed by thermodynamic calculations in consideration of phase stability between bcc and fcc phases. The resultantly formed bcc martensite favorably contributes to the transformation-induced plasticity, thereby leading to a significant enhancement in both strength and ductility as well as strain hardening. We reveal the microstructural evolutions according to the Co-Ni balance and their contributions to a mechanical response. The Co-Ni balance plays a leading role in phase stability and consequently tunes the cryogenic-temperature strength-ductility balance. The main difference from recently-reported metastable high-entropy dual-phase alloys is the formation of bcc martensite as a daughter phase, which shows significant effects on strain hardening. The hcp phase in the present MEA mostly acts as a nucleation site for the bcc martensite. Our findings demonstrate that the fcc to bcc transformation can be an attractive route to a new MEA design strategy for improving cryogenic strength-ductility.

AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

candidates.hypothesis: Applying severe plastic deformation (SPD) processing to refine the grain structure of NbMoTaW will enhance room-temperature ductility and irradiation damage tolerance via an increased grain boundary area acting as defect sinks, while largely preserving its high-temperature performance.
candidates.intervention: Process the alloy using high-pressure torsion (HPT) at room temperature followed by a short low-temperature annealing treatment designed to relieve internal stresses while retaining an ultrafine grain structure. To mitigate grain growth at high temperature, a minor addition of a grain-growth inhibitor (e.g., trace refractory oxide) may be incorporated.
candidates.changes: Added strategies to mitigate grain growth at high temperature such as the potential incorporation of minimal stabilizing additions, and specified that SPD parameters should be optimized based on prior work to ensure thermal stability.

candidates.hypothesis: Minor Hf addition to NbMoTaW will introduce nanoscopically dispersed HCP precipitates that improve room‐temperature ductility and enhance irradiation defect recombination while preserving the high‐temperature BCC strength.

candidates.changes: Explicitly detailed the processing method to ensure uniform interstitial nitrogen incorporation and added clarification on avoiding nitride formation, along with outlining measurement strategies to determine optimal nitrogen concentration.
